\begin{frontmatter}

\title{Medora: a consent-gated assistive-AI layer over an open Bangladesh medicine
reference for bilingual health-record software}

\author{Sarwad Hasan Siddiqui}
\author{Adiba Tahsin}
\author{Kazi Saeed Alam\corref{cor1}}
\ead{saeed.alam@cse.kuet.ac.bd}
\cortext[cor1]{Corresponding author.}
\address{Department of Computer Science and Engineering, Khulna University of Engineering \& Technology, Khulna 9203, Bangladesh}

\begin{abstract}
Assistive language models are entering health software faster than the structures meant
to contain them. Medora is open-source research software that makes those structures
explicit, combining bilingual English/Bangla patient-held records and appointment
coordination with an assistive-AI layer of twenty-one endpoints. Its safety properties
are structural rather than prompt-dependent: external calls require a purpose-specific
revocable grant and pass bilingual redaction and pseudonymisation; assistant navigation
resolves through an immutable role-scoped route registry that fixes the reachable
destination set at build time and excludes administrative routes; and summary items can
cite only records the backend supplied. Safety-critical routing is deterministic, with
models confined to phrasing and structured extraction. Underneath sits an open Bangladesh
medicine reference --- 7{,}389 drugs, 67{,}001 brands, a 74{,}390-term index --- built
from five published datasets by a deterministic script. We report redaction, navigation,
grounding, and booking-contention results, and state which parts carry no evaluation.
Medora is not clinically validated and is not a medical device.
\end{abstract}

\begin{keyword}
digital health \sep assistive AI \sep consent \sep medicine reference data \sep
deterministic intent routing \sep bilingual software \sep reproducibility
\end{keyword}
\end{frontmatter}

\section{Motivation and significance}

Medora addresses a practical research problem: how can a bilingual web platform put
language-model assistance in front of patients and clinicians without letting it become
unreviewed clinical authority? Assistive features are cheap to add and hard to bound, and
the bounding is where the engineering difficulty sits. The intended users are
health-informatics researchers, software-engineering educators, and teams studying
consent, assistive-AI containment, or concurrency.

Bangladesh has a long-running national digital-health program, but studies describe
uneven eHealth implementation and clinician concerns about electronic-record
adoption~\cite{ahmed2014,khan2012}. This motivates an inspectable artifact for bilingual,
patient-held workflows; it does not establish that Medora is representative of Bangladesh
or suitable for deployment.

Two contributions carry most of the reuse value. The first is an open medicine reference
for a market that lacks one. Drug terminology services such as RxNorm underpin much
clinical software, but their coverage is national and Bangladesh is not among the markets
served~\cite{rxnorm}. Medora consolidates five published datasets into a normalized
three-table reference and ships the deterministic script that builds it.

The second is a containment pattern for assistive AI. Consent is checked before a call
leaves the deployment. Assistant navigation resolves against a fixed registry, so the set
of destinations a model can reach is enumerable by reading one file and cannot be extended
at inference time. Summary source references are attached by the backend after schema
validation, making a fabricated citation structurally impossible rather than merely
unlikely. Most safety-critical logic is deterministic (Table~\ref{tab:components}): models
supply phrasing and structured extraction, while routing, red-flag detection, specialty
fallback, and dosage parsing involve no model at all.

Established open-source systems cover a wider institutional scope: OpenMRS, Bahmni, and
GNU Health provide modular medical-record, hospital, laboratory, and Fast Healthcare
Interoperability Resources (FHIR) capabilities~\cite{openmrs,bahmni,gnuhealth}. Medora
supplies a smaller mobile-oriented implementation linking patient-held records and booking
with an inspectable assistive-AI layer. These are complements, not performance baselines.

Clinical summarization work shows that fluency is not enough: faithfulness and
traceability must be evaluated separately~\cite{shing2021,tracsum}. Symptom-checker
studies report wide variation in diagnostic and urgency
recommendations~\cite{wallace2022}. Medora therefore avoids diagnosis and triage, offering
specialty candidates for navigation, preserving manual browsing, and running deterministic
emergency rules before any model call.

\section{Software description}

\subsection{Software architecture}

Medora comprises a Next.js web client, a FastAPI core API, a separate FastAPI OCR
service, and PostgreSQL (Fig.~\ref{fig:trust}). Authentication identifies the actor;
backend role, ownership, care-relationship, appointment-state, and consent checks
authorize each operation. Frontend visibility is only a usability aid.

Because those predicates live in the API, they hold only while the API is the sole path to
the data. A release audit found it was not: the managed database also exposed a direct
data API on which every application table granted full read and write access to the
anonymous role with row-level security disabled, so the browser-published anonymous key
reached patient rows without traversing any check above. The permission matrix and its
negative tests had never covered that path because they exercised the API alone. The
release revokes those grants, enables row-level security on every table as a second
barrier, and narrows the client's only direct subscription to a trigger-maintained change
feed. An authorization model expressed only in application code is contingent on the
database exposing no second door --- an assumption deserving an explicit test.

\begin{figure}[!h]
\centering\resizebox{\textwidth}{!}{\input{figures-src/trust_boundary.tex}}
\caption{Deployment and trust boundaries. Local speech recognition and OCR do not cross
an external-processing boundary. Hosted text models, Vapi live audio, and Azure document
OCR are distinct recipients with separate grants.}
\label{fig:trust}
\end{figure}

Processing is deny-by-default (Fig.~\ref{fig:consent}). A grant records subject,
recipient, purpose, scopes, policy version, validity, grant and revocation times, and
audit metadata. Missing, expired, revoked, or wrong-scope grants produce a typed denial
and offer a local path where one exists. Revocation blocks later processing but cannot
retract prior disclosure, and local mode never falls back to a cloud service.

\begin{figure}[!h]
\centering\resizebox{\textwidth}{!}{\input{figures-src/consent_flow.tex}}
\caption{Consent-aware processing. The named purpose and provider are checked before
external processing; all outputs remain non-authoritative drafts.}
\label{fig:consent}
\end{figure}

\subsection{Software functionalities}

\textbf{Medicine reference.} Medicine identity is the substrate the platform depends on:
search, medication linking, prescription composition, and matching of recognised
prescription text all resolve through it. Five published datasets are normalized by a
deterministic, published script into three tables (Table~\ref{tab:corpus}):
\texttt{drugs}, canonical identity keyed on generic name, strength, and dosage form and
immutable after creation; \texttt{brands}, mapping commercial names --- what a prescriber
writes --- many-to-one onto those identities; and \texttt{medicine\_search\_index},
flattening both into one trigram-indexed term space for typo-tolerant lookup. The
reference exposes no dosage logic, interaction checking, or effectiveness ranking; these
are explicit non-goals.

\centering\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}lr@{}}
\toprule
Artifact & Count \\
\midrule
Consolidated source rows & 71{,}795 \\
Canonical drugs (generic $\times$ strength $\times$ form) & 7{,}389 \\
Brand entries & 67{,}001 \\

Distinct generic names & 5{,}242 \\
Distinct brand names & 52{,}117 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Medicine reference as loaded. Counts differ from the consolidated CSV because
the canonical key collapses brand duplicates and the index carries both generic and brand

\label{tab:corpus}
\end{table}

\textbf{Assistive-AI layer.} Twenty-one endpoints expose assistive features
(Table~\ref{tab:ai-surface}), all sharing one pipeline built from the components in
Table~\ref{tab:components}. A single orchestrator is the only component aware of which
provider is configured --- Groq, Gemini, Cerebras, or a deterministic mock for
reproducible testing. It recursively sanitizes input, issues the call under a random
correlation identifier rather than a stable subject token, validates the response against
a Pydantic model, and records latency and provider metadata. Raw prompts, transcripts, and
findings are not logged by default, and validation failure raises rather than degrading to
unvalidated prose.

Three guards precede the orchestrator. A consent guard reads the patient's data-sharing
state, returns permitted categories, filters the payload, and prepends a restriction
notice when anything was removed, so the model is told it is reasoning over a partial
record. A redaction stage removes emails, telephone numbers, addresses, national and
passport identifiers, account numbers, and dates in both scripts. A pseudonymiser
substitutes a stable opaque patient reference, so raw identifiers reach neither provider
nor audit log. Doctor-to-patient reads are further gated on an existing care relationship
and written to a patient-visible audit.

Chorui, the in-app assistant, is the clearest instance of the containment pattern
(Fig.~\ref{fig:chorui}). An utterance is normalized to a canonical intent, then resolved
against an immutable tuple of typed registry entries binding intent and role scope to a
route, its required parameters, and a fallback. The registry holds 24 entries over 23
canonical intents, 11 patient-scoped and 11 doctor-scoped with 2 shared; administrative
routes are never registered. Missing parameters yield a clarification rather than a guess.
Destinations are therefore fixed at build time and auditable from one file, unlike
free-form tool selection where the prompt is the only control.

\begin{figure}[!h]
\centering\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures-src/chorui_architecture.pdf}
\caption{Chorui request path. Intent normalization and registry resolution are
deterministic; the model contributes phrasing and structured content, not the set of
reachable destinations.}
\label{fig:chorui}
\end{figure}

Summaries for patients, prescribers, and prescription histories are read-only. Source
references are collected by the backend and attached after schema validation, so an item
can cite only a record the request supplied; a request carrying no source record yields an
explicit not-found item rather than model prose. Record timestamps are stripped before the
prompt leaves the deployment, so the model cannot reason about temporal order. A
clinician-verification warning stays visible and there is no automatic writeback.

Local faster-whisper transcription is preloaded at startup and crosses no external
boundary~\cite{whisper}; only the structuring step involves a hosted model. Vapi live
audio is a separate external recipient requiring its own grant at capture and again when
callbacks are processed, and local mode never escalates to it automatically.

Table~\ref{tab:ai-surface} states the evaluation position directly, because it is this
release's main limitation. Structural controls apply uniformly across all twenty-one
endpoints; empirical evidence does not. Three groups carry reproducible fixtures; the
remaining six are exercised by contract and authorization tests but carry no accuracy or
faithfulness measurement, and none should be inferred.

\textbf{Reviewable clinical semantics.} Nothing the layer produces is authoritative.
Summaries are drafts; prescription suggestions pre-fill fields a prescriber edits and
signs; specialty search returns candidates with uncertainty and manual browse controls.
Recognised prescription images return an unconfirmed draft carrying mode, provider,
confidence, warnings, and \texttt{authoritative\_writeback=false}, and a person must
verify every row before it affects medication records. A patient's later action is
\texttt{receipt\_acknowledged} or \texttt{discrepancy\_reported}; neither means a medicine
is appropriate. The service worker caches only versioned static and public resources,
health-data writes are not background-synchronized, and logout clears Medora caches,
IndexedDB, session storage, and sensitive local storage.

\textbf{Appointment transaction and delivery.} Creating an appointment requires an
\texttt{Idempotency-Key}. The backend locks the key and slot, validates availability, and
writes the appointment, idempotency result, audit record, and outbox event in one
transaction; a uniqueness constraint is the last defense against duplicate active slots.
Only committed outbox events are published (Fig.~\ref{fig:booking}). Realtime messages
improve responsiveness; after reconnect, clients query PostgreSQL because it remains
authoritative.

\caption{Booking timeline. Transaction consistency ends at commit; notification and
realtime propagation are later events and are measured separately.}
\label{fig:booking}
\end{figure}

\subsection{Evaluation and reproducibility}

Evaluation covers the privacy stack, the two AI behaviours with defined correctness
criteria, and booking concurrency. Mock and live provider results are never pooled.

The privacy suite is a hand-authored synthetic bilingual corpus spanning labelled and
unlabelled names, contact and address details, national, passport and account
identifiers, clinician details, dates, mixed-script records, spacing and misspelling
variants, obfuscated formats, over-redaction controls, consent state, and prompt
injection. Cases are deliberately not derived from the redaction patterns they test, so
precision and recall fall below 100\%: unlabelled personal names, clinician names in
prose, month-name dates, and obfuscated contact formats are not detected. Each such case
carries a written limitation in the archived results, and the release gate fails on any
undisclosed failure. Reporting recall of 75.5\% rather than tuning the corpus upward is
deliberate --- it describes what the redactor detects on inputs it was not built against,
the only figure that transfers to a deployment.

Navigation fixtures are scored on two paths, a recorded provider intent and the
deterministic mock, against the same classifier the request path uses. Uncertainty is a
flag reported alongside candidates rather than a fourth exclusive class, and manual
browsing is asserted to remain available on every path. The red-flag rules are keyword
based and match negated, third-person, and historical mentions, so they over-trigger
toward emergency guidance; those cases are enumerated. Summary fixtures invoke the
summarizer end to end under the mock provider and assert that no item cites a record
identifier the backend did not supply, that a request with no source record yields an
explicit not-found item, and that malformed output raises rather than degrades.

Booking contention runs at 2, 10, and 50 concurrent attempts for 30 fresh-slot
repetitions per level after warm-up, requiring one committed appointment, no duplicate
row, stable idempotent replay, rollback-safe retry, and post-commit outbox processing.
Transaction and propagation latency are separate outputs.

\IfFileExists{generated/safety_results.tex}{\input{generated/safety_results.tex}}{}
\IfFileExists{generated/booking_results.tex}{\input{generated/booking_results.tex}}{}

The provider manifest records provider, model, interface version, region, temperature,
context limit, timeout, retries, fallback policy, execution date, retention assumption,
and paid-service requirement. Installation commands, model and image checksums, raw
output, and table-generation instructions accompany the archive.

\textbf{Prescription image OCR: a negative result.} An experimental pipeline recognises
photographed prescriptions and matches the results against the medicine reference,
combining region detection, a local or cloud recognition backend, a dosage grammar,
Bangla normalization, and fuzzy catalog matching~\cite{du2020,prescriptionocr}. On
handwritten Bangladeshi prescriptions its output is not reliable enough to serve even as
a draft: recognition quality on cursive prescriber handwriting is the binding constraint,
and fuzzy matching against a 67{,}001-entry brand space converts a partially recognised
token into a confident wrong match as readily as a correct one. Raising the threshold
trades those errors for empty results rather than removing them. Review gating keeps every
incorrect extraction out of the medication record, so the cost is wasted reviewer effort
rather than clinical risk --- but a draft a reviewer must rewrite is not a working
feature. We therefore make no accuracy claim and publish no OCR benchmark; independent
labelling, adjudication, and a held-out evaluation remain prerequisites for any future
claim. The pipeline stays in the codebase because the failure locates the difficulty in
handwriting recognition and large-catalog disambiguation, not in the surrounding software.

\section{Illustrative examples}

\textit{Assistant boundary.} A doctor has an active care relationship and a valid
\texttt{specialty\_navigation} grant for the named mock provider. ``Patient name: Test
Rahim; phone: 01700000000'' becomes ``Patient name: [redacted-name]; phone:
[redacted-phone]'' before the schema-gated request. The response offers Dermatology as an
uncertain candidate, explains that it is not a diagnosis, and preserves manual browsing.
A follow-up asking for a diagnosis and prescription returns a safe refusal. Inputs,
authorization state, schema, intermediate values, and outputs are archived in
\texttt{tests/benchmarks/datasets/worked\_examples.json}.

\textit{Registry containment.} A patient asks the assistant to open the admin dashboard.
No administrative route exists in the registry, so resolution produces no destination and
the engine returns its fallback. The outcome does not depend on the model declining: there
is no entry it could have selected, and the same holds for a prompt-injected attempt to
name the route directly.

\textit{Consent restriction.} A doctor requests a summary for a patient who has shared
conditions and medications but not test results. The consent guard removes the laboratory
category, the payload carries a restriction notice into the prompt, and the summary
reports the omission rather than inferring around it. The access is written to the
patient-visible audit table.

\section{Impact}

Medora is a compact test bed for studying assistive-AI containment, consent state
machines, source traceability, and transaction/event boundaries in one system. The
medicine reference and its build script are reusable independently of the platform, and
the deterministic mock provider makes interface and failure tests reproducible without
paid credentials. The registry pattern transfers: any assistant navigating a role-scoped
application can bound its action set the same way.

The limitations are substantial. Most of the assistive surface is unevaluated: six of the
nine groups in Table~\ref{tab:ai-surface} carry no accuracy or faithfulness measurement,
and the structural controls applying to them are not evidence that their outputs are good.
The medicine reference is a consolidation of third-party datasets --- two of them website
scrapes --- not an authoritative register; it has not been validated against any
regulatory source, its indication text has had no clinical review, and coverage reflects
its sources' collection dates. Structured redaction misses unknown and indirect
identifiers, emergency rules cannot cover every presentation, summaries and specialty
candidates may omit or distort facts, and prescription OCR does not work well enough to
use. Provider behavior, cost, and retention can change. The concurrency benchmark
demonstrates database behavior in its tested environment, not universal capacity. No
clinical trial, regulatory assessment, penetration test, or independent clinical
validation has been completed. Any real deployment needs local governance, security
review, professional oversight, and validation for its intended use.

\section{Ethics and data availability}
\label{sec:ethics}

Code is released under the MIT License; annotations, synthetic fixtures, and aggregate
results under CC BY 4.0.

The medicine reference consolidates five sources licensed CC0 1.0 (two), Apache 2.0, MIT,
and CC BY 4.0~\cite{bdmeds}, all permitting redistribution. The corpus is offered under
CC BY 4.0, the most restrictive term in the set, with a notice crediting every source;
Apache 2.0's statement-of-changes requirement is met by recording that generic names were
normalized, only the generic-to-indication mapping retained, and pricing and URL fields
discarded. Two sources are website scrapes whose uploaders did not author the material,
which is why the corpus is described as a consolidation of community-published data rather
than an authoritative register.

The prescription image corpus is not deposited. It is identifiable medical material; its
consent basis is verbal agreement obtained for an undergraduate software project; no
institutional review board reviewed the collection; and the evaluation it was assembled to
support is not part of this release. Consent for a student project is not informed consent
for permanent worldwide publication. The images retain patient and clinician names,
registration numbers, and clinic details, and handwriting is quasi-biometric, so redacting
direct identifiers would reduce but not eliminate re-identification risk. The corpus, its
data-use notice, and its per-record provenance classification remain in the repository
under a notice prohibiting re-identification and unauthorized secondary use. Any future
deposit requires documented consent or controlled access.

\section{Conclusions}

Medora is research software for bilingual patient-held records, appointment coordination,
and assistive AI bounded by construction rather than by instruction. Its reusable
contributions are an open Bangladesh medicine reference with a published deterministic
build, and a containment pattern in which consent is checked before a call leaves the
deployment, navigation resolves against an immutable registry, and generated clinical text
can cite only backend-supplied records. We report what is measured and name what is not.
Medora should be judged as an inspectable platform for software research, not as a
clinically validated or production-ready medical system.
